inline.s: Among the four marks, the mark of a self comes first. Once this mark is set up, the other three marks arise in response. Thereupon selfishness, private advantage, and private desire surge up, and affliction and karmic retribution follow along. To catch the bandits, first catch their ringleader: for a student of Buddhism the first thing to break is the mark of a self, because when there is a mark of a self, there are the marks of a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan. If there is no mark of a self, then there are no marks at all; the very substance is empty and still, and all wisdom naturally appears before one.
In the

Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma, Chapter Three, “Recollection of the Dharma,” the Buddha says: “Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings free of inversion who contemplate things as they truly are, they have right view. If one gives rise to the thought of a self, the thought of a person, or the thought of a sentient being, you should know that such a person walks the wrong path. Śāriputra! The Buddha and his disciples do not speak of a self, do not speak of a person, do not speak of a sentient being, do not speak of a lifespan, do not speak of annihilation or permanence; therefore the Buddha and his disciples are called those of right view. Why is that? Because their contemplation is right and free of inversion.” This shows that one who holds such wrong views as the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan does not even qualify to be a disciple of the Buddha—how much less to be a bodhisattva! In the Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma the World-Honored One sets forth this principle, and the true nature of all dharmas, in exhaustive detail.

[The two views of annihilation and permanence] The “view of annihilation” holds that the self is limited to a single lifetime and that after death everything ceases to be. The “view of permanence” holds that after death the self is not destroyed but is reborn and continues in its present form—for example, one who is born human is human life after life, and one born a dog is a dog life after life. Right view is this: free of annihilation and free of permanence, and taking the Middle Way, the true nature of things.
Question: How are the four marks to be transcended?

Answer: This can be done in two steps. First, do not mistake this body-and-mind of the five aggregates and all conditions for something real and thus cling to them. In the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra of the Mahāyāna the Buddha says: “If practitioners give rise to the clinging to existence or non-existence with regard to objects (if, toward objects, they give rise to the clinging to existence or to non-existence—clinging that things are or that they are not, as when one wrongly holds that an ox has horns and a hare does not), then they are caught in the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan.” Second, once you already have the power to let a thought arise without continuing it, freedom from the four marks is freedom from the four conceptualizations. The marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan are simply the thoughts of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan that surface in your mind; this is why some translations of the Diamond Sutra render the four marks as the four conceptualizations. Kumārajīva’s (350–413) translation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says: “If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva.” But the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s (499–569) translation of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says: “All bodhisattvas are free of the conceptualization of a self, the conceptualization of a sentient being, the conceptualization of a lifespan, and the conceptualization of a receiver.” Therefore, whenever a thought about a self, a person, a sentient being, or a lifespan surfaces, you must immediately extinguish it (when your skill in contemplating the mind is deep, you can do this), and on no account let it continue and become a conceptualization; you must reach the point where a thought arising is immediately noticed, and once noticed it is gone. The Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma says: “The buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is entirely without conceptualization and without thought.” The Essentials of Mind Transmission says: “To stir the mind and move a thought is to depart from the Dharma-substance and to grasp at marks; since beginningless time there has never been a Buddha who grasped at marks.”

“Wondrous practice without dwelling”: “without dwelling” here means knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore neither grasping at conditions nor becoming defiled—acting without being attached to the action (free of love and hate, grasping and rejecting); this is called wondrous practice. “Wondrous practice without dwelling” is the giving without dwelling in marks spoken of below. Not dwelling in marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; giving without dwelling in marks is the dual practice of compassion and emptiness. This section answers the question “How should one dwell?”—one dwells (abides) by giving without dwelling in marks, which answers from afar the World-Honored One’s words in Section Two, “one should dwell thus.”

[Without dwelling] Not grasping at marks. That is to say, with regard to the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, a lifespan, dharmas, and non-dharmas, one dwells nowhere (one does not wrongly cling to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Free of marks, there is no-mark; with no-mark, there is no dwelling; with no dwelling, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”

[Grasping at marks] Grasping at marks is taking marks as real, so that desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desire and thought. Thus one creates karma, and thus there is birth-and-death and transmigration. Therefore, do not cling to marks as real and be moved by them. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at marks, and thus unmoved.”

Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere—that is, give without dwelling in form, and give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas. Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks.

This passage comes right after the World-Honored One has finished answering the second question, “How should one subdue the mind?” and immediately answers the first question as well. Subhūti asked, “How should one dwell?” The World-Honored One answers, “Give without dwelling in marks.” That is, a bodhisattva should give free of marks, with the three wheels emptied; this is how one dwells—that is, one dwells (abides) by giving without dwelling in marks.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
—Moreover, Subhūti! Having answered “How should one subdue the mind?” the World-Honored One immediately goes on to answer the question “How should one dwell?” (how should one abide?).
A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere.”

—A bodhisattva should give free of marks, and in giving must not cling to objects and give rise to thoughts, nor be turned by objects. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought is free of objects, that is bodhi.”

Dharma” has several meanings: first, it broadly refers to all things and matters, including thought, speech, and writing, all of which are called “dharmas”; second, law or principle; third, method; fourth, the Dharma of the Way, that is, the principles, methods, and realms of cultivating the Way; fifth, mental objects, the dharmas among the six dusts (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas). Which meaning is intended must be judged from the context. In the sentence “A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere,” “dharmas” broadly refers to all things. [Dwelling nowhere with regard to dharmas] Knowing that all dharmas are empty, and therefore neither grasping at conditions nor becoming defiled.

Giving” means giving to others what one has. There are three kinds of giving: the giving of wealth, relieving the sick, weak, poor, and suffering with material goods; the giving of Dharma, guiding others out of suffering with the right Dharma; and the giving of fearlessness, freeing others from terror and dread.
That is, give without dwelling in form, and give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.”

—This explains the preceding sentence, “A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should give with a mind that dwells nowhere.” Concretely, it means giving without dwelling in the dust of form, giving without dwelling in the dust of sound, giving without dwelling in the dust of fragrance, giving without dwelling in the dust of taste, giving without dwelling in the dust of touch, and giving without dwelling in the dust of dharmas.

Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas” are called the six dusts—the dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of fragrance, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of dharmas. “Dust” means defilement: it can defile the human mind so that self-nature cannot manifest. They are also called the six objects, that is, the objects grasped at by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind): the eye sees form, the ear hears sound, the nose smells fragrance, the tongue tastes flavor, the body feels touch, and the mind knows dharmas. “Without dwelling” here means having no love or hate, no grasping or rejecting, toward the objects of the dusts (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas).

The first five dusts (the dusts of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch) include every material object within the reach of the senses, while the dust of dharmas includes every mental object within the reach of the mind. Thus the six words “form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, dharmas” refer to all objects, and the words in Section Ten, “one should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas,” mean that no object whatsoever may be clung to. When the Buddha speaks of the six dusts, he always mentions form first and then follows with sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, because the dust of form (what the eye sees) most easily deludes people and has the greatest influence among the six dusts; therefore he singles it out first as a warning.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices,
giving comes first, and giving without dwelling encompasses the remaining five pāramitās. In the

Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter One, “The Prologue,” the Buddha says: “Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving with prajñāpāramitā (that is, giving without dwelling), by the power of wisdom and skillful means he can fulfill the pāramitā of dāna (giving), the pāramitā of śīla (observing precepts), the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience), the pāramitā of vīrya (diligence), the pāramitā of dhyāna (meditative concentration), and the pāramitā of prajñā (wisdom). Śāriputra said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when giving, by the power of wisdom and skillful means fulfills the pāramitā of dāna and on through the pāramitā of prajñā? The Buddha told Śāriputra: Because giver, receiver, and material goods are ungraspable (the three wheels are empty), one can fulfill the pāramitā of dāna. Because guilt and guiltlessness are ungraspable, one fulfills the pāramitā of śīla. Because the mind is unmoved, one fulfills the pāramitā of kṣānti. Because body and mind are diligent without slackening, one fulfills the pāramitā of vīrya. Because one is neither scattered nor dull, one fulfills the pāramitā of dhyāna. Because one knows all dharmas to be ungraspable, one fulfills the pāramitā of prajñā.”
In the

Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, Chapter Two, “Learning and Contemplation,” the Buddha says: “All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate prajñāpāramitā can know things as they truly are: if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, taking non-attainment as skillful means, cultivates the pāramitā of giving, and understands that all givers, receivers, and gifts are ungraspable, then such giving, skillful and wise, can fulfill the pāramitās of giving, pure precepts, patient acceptance, diligence, meditative stillness, and prajñā.”

[The six pāramitās] Also called the six pāramitās: the six Dharma-gates by which one may cross from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss—namely giving, observing precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving can carry one across stinginess and greed; observing precepts can carry one across transgression; patience can carry one across anger; diligence can carry one across slackness; meditative concentration can carry one across distraction; prajñā can carry one across delusion. [The six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices] In brief they are the six pāramitās; in full they are the ten thousand practices, and the six pāramitās include every practice a bodhisattva cultivates.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks.”

—The World-Honored One emphasizes once again: one should give in this way, without dwelling in marks (without giving rise to a discriminating mind toward marks). For giving is meant to use illusion to transcend illusion, not to use illusion to enter further into illusion; it is meant to dissolve the self, not to inflate the self. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “To have a self is itself the fault; to forget one’s own merit is a blessing beyond compare.”
Why is that? If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.

The World-Honored One explains why “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”: because “if a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are inconceivable.” That is, the merit and virtue of giving without dwelling in marks are utterly vast—so vast that the mind cannot even imagine them.

The Four Lessons of Liaofan says: When one does good and the mind does not cling to the good, then whatever one accomplishes is brought to perfection; when the mind clings to the good, then even a lifetime of diligent effort stops at half-good. Suppose, for example, one relieves others with wealth: inwardly one does not see a self, outwardly one does not see a person, and in between one does not see the thing given—this is called the three wheels being empty, this is called the mind of single purity; then a single measure of grain can plant boundless blessings, and a single coin can erase the offenses of a thousand kalpas. But if this mind is not forgotten (if one still clings to the good), then even ten thousand yi of gold will not bring merit to fullness. Long ago a certain woman came to a temple wishing to give but having no wealth; she had only two coins, which she donated, and the abbot himself performed the repentance for her. Later she entered the palace and became rich and noble, and she brought several thousand in gold to the temple to give; the abbot merely had his disciples dedicate the merit. She therefore asked: When I gave two coins before, the master himself performed the repentance for me; now I give several thousand in gold, and the master does not dedicate the merit. Why is this? He said: Before, though the gift was small, the mind of giving was utterly sincere, and nothing short of my own repentance could repay the virtue; now, though the gift is large, the mind of giving is not as earnest as it was then, and having others repent on your behalf is enough.
What follows explains how inconceivable is the merit and virtue of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling in marks.

Subhūti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhūti! Can the space in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One. Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are likewise inconceivable. Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught.
Subhūti! What do you think? Can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One.”
—The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can the vastness of the space stretching away to the east be measured? Subhūti answers: It cannot be measured, World-Honored One!

Can it be measured? No.” Both instances of the character rendered “No” here carry the old reading that means “not so”; in classical Chinese this character is interchangeable with the word for “not so.” Throughout the entire sutra Subhūti answers “No” in more than ten places, and in every case it carries the clear sense of a negative, and so it is read as “not so”; read in the customary way as “it is not,” it also works.
Subhūti! Can the space in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One.”

—The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can the vastness of the space stretching away along the south, the west, the north, the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest, as well as above and below, be measured? Subhūti answers: It cannot be measured, World-Honored One!
[The four intermediate directions] Southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest are called the four intermediate directions.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are likewise inconceivable.”

—The World-Honored One says: Subhūti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are as vast and boundless as the space of the ten directions (east, south, west, and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below), and cannot be measured.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught.”
—Therefore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply abide by the teaching I have set out above (practicing the six pāramitās without giving rise to a discriminating mind toward marks).

Here it is made clear that what was said above answers the question “How should one dwell?” The “dwell” here means to abide, and it differs in meaning from the “dwell” in “give without dwelling in form, give without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.” In that phrase, “dwell” means the mind abiding in objects and thereby giving rise to discrimination and clinging, arousing love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and being turned by objects.
At this point the World-Honored One has answered Subhūti’s two great questions:
Question: How should one subdue the mind? Answer: By delivering all sentient beings without dwelling in marks.

Question: How should one dwell? Answer: “Give without dwelling in marks.” Not dwelling in marks is emptiness; giving is compassion; compassion and emptiness are practiced together, and giving without dwelling in marks encompasses the entire six pāramitās—this is the bodhisattva path.
Question: How do we know that this section answers “How should one dwell?”
Answer: At the end of this section, when summing up this teaching, the World-Honored One says: “Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply dwell as he has been taught (as taught above).”
Question: Why does the World-Honored One not answer the first question first?

Answer: Because the answer to the second question, “How should one subdue the mind?”, is the making of a great vow—to deliver all sentient beings without dwelling in marks—while the answer to “How should one dwell?” is great practice—to give without dwelling in marks. Great practice is built upon the foundation of the great vow, and so the World-Honored One first speaks of the great vow and then of the great practice.
Question: How can one actually give without dwelling in marks?

Answer: This is what Section Ten teaches: “One should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

Seeing reality as it is” is what the passage of this section means by “if you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.” In this section the World-Honored One further clarifies: Why is it that “thus I deliver immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet not a single sentient being is delivered”? Why must there be no mark of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a lifespan? Why is it that “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”? Because: “All that has marks is illusory and false.” And further: “If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.”

[If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata] If, on seeing all marks, you understand (and this is not a verbal understanding) that they are illusory marks, then you see your own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathāgata).
Subhūti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of bodily marks?
The World-Honored One asks: Subhūti! What do you think—can sentient beings, dwelling and clinging to their own physical body (bodily marks), see their own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathāgata)?
[Dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body] Wrongly clinging to the physical body as real and taking it to be oneself.

[Intrinsic nature] Intrinsic nature is also called Buddha-nature, the original face, and suchness. Because intrinsic nature is Buddha, it is called Buddha-nature; because intrinsic nature is the original state of self-nature, it is called the original face, also shortened to “the original”; because intrinsic nature is the original state of self-nature, unchanging and constant, it is called suchness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Intrinsic nature is Buddha; apart from the nature there is no other Buddha.”
For a detailed discussion of intrinsic nature, see
“Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha”
. [Bodily marks]
This refers to a sentient being’s own physical body.
Older commentaries take

bodily marks” to mean the Buddha’s thirty-two marks. To this, Upāsaka Jiang Weihuang’s Lectures on the Diamond Sutra points out: would such an interpretation not repeat the later passage on the thirty-two marks? Every word and every sentence of the Diamond Sutra has deep meaning; there is certainly no repetition.
The two characters “bodily marks” here should be taken as referring to a sentient being’s physical body.

The Buddha’s meaning in this passage is: You sentient beings—can you, by means of your own bodily marks, see your intrinsic nature? [Would such an interpretation not repeat the later passage on the thirty-two marks]
In the later Section Thirteen, “Upholding the Dharma as Taught,” the sutra says:

“Subhūti! What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is that? What the Tathāgata speaks of as the thirty-two marks are no-marks, and so they are called the thirty-two marks.”
Of all the principles set out in the preceding passages, the most essential is the repeated clarification that one should not dwell in marks. For example:

“Thus I deliver immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, and yet not a single sentient being is delivered,” “if a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, then he is not a bodhisattva,” “a bodhisattva should give in this way, without dwelling in marks”

, and so on. Why, then, should one not dwell in marks? Because only by not dwelling in marks can one realize intrinsic nature. To realize it in part is to be a bodhisattva of the first ground, no longer retreating from the mind of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; to realize it to the fullest is to become a Buddha. And among all marks, what sentient beings care about most and cling to most is their own physical body (bodily marks)—this is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating. Therefore the World-Honored One here asks in a way meant to awaken them: Can sentient beings, clinging to the physical body, see their intrinsic nature? This is breaking the view of the body.
[Clinging to the physical body is the root cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, wrongly taking the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadows cast by the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person wrongly clings to them, and because of that wrong clinging he is not only deluded about the nature of this space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence comes the turning round in birth-and-death, and so it is called ignorance.”

[Translation: Since beginningless time all sentient beings have had their self-nature deluded and inverted, giving rise to all kinds of inversion and taking the false as real—this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings and takes north for south and east for west: he wrongly takes the flesh formed by the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own body, and the deliberating mind of the six faculties as they contact the six dusts (the shadows cast by the six dusts) as the mark of his own mind. It is like a diseased eye falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. In truth there are no flowers in the sky; they are an illusion wrongly clung to by the diseased eye, and because of that wrong clinging one not only wrongly clings to space as real but also believes that the flowers truly arise from there. Because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, they wrongly take the illusory body and mind to be real and cling to them as a self, and so birth-and-death and transmigration never cease; this is what is called ignorance.]
[The view of the body] The wrong view that clings to the body as real.
No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks. Why is that? What the Tathāgata speaks of as bodily marks are no bodily marks.

Subhūti answers: No, World-Honored One! One cannot see intrinsic nature by dwelling and clinging to one’s own physical body. Why is that? Because what the Tathāgata speaks of as the physical body (the mark exists) is no physical body (the substance is void); therefore the physical body is illusory, and one must not cling in delusion to the illusory physical body as real and thus see one’s own intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Subhūti: All that has marks is illusory and false.
The World-Honored One further teaches Subhūti: Not only is the physical body (bodily marks) an illusion—all marks whatsoever are also illusions.
[All that has marks is illusory and false] All marks are illusions. In the article
“The True Nature of All Dharmas”
this is set out in detail.
Great Master Guifeng says:

“That all dharmas are like a dream, all the sages say with one voice. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the objects of the dusts are originally empty. The mind of emptiness and stillness is not obscured in its spiritual knowing. This knowing of emptiness and stillness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all wonders. Because of beginningless delusion about it, one wrongly clings to body and mind as a self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and anger. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of emptiness and stillness. Knowing is without thought and without form—who then is the mark of a self or the mark of a person? Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies nowhere but here. Therefore, though one undertakes the ten thousand practices in full, one takes no-thought alone as the guiding principle. Once one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought, love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase in clarity, karmic offenses are naturally cut off, and one’s practice naturally advances. Since one understands that all marks are no-marks, there is naturally the cultivation that is no cultivation. When affliction is exhausted, birth-and-death ceases. When birth and extinction are extinguished, still illumination appears before one, and its responsive function is inexhaustible; this is called Buddha.”

(From the Preface to the Collected Writings on the Sources of Chan.) [Awakening to all marks as empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; once aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies nowhere but here] Awakening to all marks as illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that one is taking the illusory as real and being turned by illusory marks. Having awakened to this, the deluded thought immediately disappears. The wondrous gate of cultivation is right here!

Here the World-Honored One tells us the ultimate truth: all marks whatsoever are neither truly existent nor entirely nonexistent, but illusory. (They are like things in a dream: not entirely nonexistent, because for the dreamer they truly occur and are truly felt; and yet not truly existent. Hence they are named with such words as illusion, falseness, and emptiness. People everywhere, because they wrongly cling to marks as real, are seduced and driven by them, give rise to delusion and create karma, and suffer transmigration to no purpose.)
All that has marks is illusory and false”—this sentence shows how to contemplate with wisdom; it is the starting point for upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Knowing the illusion, one is immediately free of it, with no need for skillful means; being free of the illusion is itself enlightenment, with no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the final age who cultivate in accordance with this can thereby forever leave all illusions behind.”

This is the crucial point for applying effort in upholding the Diamond Sutra: be free of the illusion! When watching a 3-D film, for instance, if a tiger suddenly lunges at you, you are startled, and then you smile knowingly: it is fake! Watch it a few more times, and you are unmoved. But in a dream, when a tiger hotly pursues you, you flee in panic and suffer unbearably, because you take it as real. This is the difference between awakening and delusion.

Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the truth of the universe and human life: all marks are illusions. On reflection, this is truly astonishing. If so, which of the myriad things in the universe is not an illusion? No wonder the World-Honored One says in Section Fourteen:
“If there is again someone who, hearing this sutra, is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such a person is most rare.”

Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have taken “marks” as real, so that the mind is turned by objects, karma is created, retribution is received, and they turn round in the six realms. Therefore the World-Honored One tells us to be free of marks. To be free of marks means: seeing marks without being deluded and without giving rise to a mind (as a mirror reflects things), not being turned by objects, knowing them to be illusions, free of love and hate, and not grasping at conditions. This is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra. The Heart Sutra says:

“Because of non-attainment, the bodhisattva, relying on prajñāpāramitā, has a mind without obstruction. Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear; far removed from inverted dream-thoughts, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa.”

Here “prajñāpāramitā” is the wondrous wisdom that clearly knows all marks to be illusory and lets them go—that is, the practice of being free of marks: seeing marks without delusion, and not being turned by objects.

All that has marks is illusory and false”—this is the reason for, and the method of, transcending the four marks (the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a lifespan): Why transcend the four marks? Because they are all false. How does one transcend the four marks? By firmly remembering that “all that has marks is illusory and false,” and letting go of the illusion the moment it is seen, with no need for skillful means.

This is like watching a television series: if you are deeply absorbed, then along with the illusory situations your love and hate, grasping and rejecting, joy and anger, sorrow and gladness never cease. This is exactly how it has been since beginningless kalpas: giving rise to delusion, creating karma, receiving retribution, and transmigrating. But if, while watching, we keep reminding ourselves—This is fake! This is fake!—and even smile faintly, we will grow more and more unmoved, until we have neither the interest nor the patience to watch the whole series of dozens of episodes. So the way to be free of marks (seeing marks without delusion, not being turned by objects) is this: constantly contemplate that “all that has marks is illusory and false,” and make it your own view, your own consciousness, speech, and action—this is to be awakening. At the same time, whenever conditions appear before you, keep reminding yourself: body, mind, and world are all illusions. In the question of whether or not you can “treat them as false and not be turned by them,” test your own awakening and skill. Contemplating and testing, testing and contemplating—this is eradicating habitual tendencies, this is breaking ignorance, this is cultivation. Do this closely and continuously, and it will be exactly as the Sixth Patriarch said: “May the disciple’s own mind constantly give rise to wisdom, and never depart from self-nature—this is the field of merit.”

To see marks without delusion is to suffer no harm from them; to see marks and fall into delusion is to invite endless trouble. Those deluded by wealth die over wealth; those deluded by fame die over fame; those deluded by form die over form.
If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.
If, on seeing all marks, you understand them all to be not real (no-marks) but illusory, and you are not moved by them, then you see your own intrinsic Buddha (the Tathāgata).

If you see all marks as no-marks,” deluded thoughts cease of themselves—this is clarifying the mind (making the mind clear); “then you see the Tathāgata”—this is seeing the nature. The sentence “If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata” is the essential path to clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.
In the
Treasury of the Buddha-Dharma, Chapter Two, “Recollection of the Buddha,” the Buddha says:
“To see the true nature of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and unpossessed.”
What is seeing the nature? To see marks and know them to be illusions, and not be turned by them, is seeing the nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch,
Chapter Two, “Prajñā,” says:
“Simply let right view constantly arise within your own mind, so that affliction and the dust of toil can never defile it—this is seeing the nature.”

In this passage the World-Honored One tells Subhūti: Not only are bodily marks illusory—all marks whatsoever are illusions. If, on seeing all marks, one recognizes them to be illusions (rather than being muddled and taking them as real), one is not turned by objects, remains perfectly at ease, and the mad mind suddenly rests; one then sees the intrinsic Buddha that everyone possesses. Clarifying the mind and seeing the nature is the heart of Buddhist study and practice. Seeing the nature is enlightenment—awakening to the fact that all dharmas are illusory. The task thereafter is: cultivating in accordance with that awakening, gradually eradicating habitual tendencies, reaching the point of not being dragged along by thoughts and not being turned by objects, and thus perfecting the fruit of the Way.

All that has marks is illusory and false. If you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata”—this teaching is tremendously important! If we now train our own minds at every moment, understanding that all marks are illusions, no longer grasping at or chasing after conditions, no longer coveting, no longer clinging, then the mind becomes utterly empty and pure. Then, once this physical body breaks up and the four elements (earth, water, fire, and wind) disperse, the consciousness will emerge and be able to take charge, and will not be turned by objects and so enter a womb. In life one is free and at ease, and after death, let illusory realms transform as they will—there is no mind to be moved. If one can be like this, one can radiate great light, illumine the ten directions, come and go freely, and respond to conditions and to the faithful wherever they are, always at ease; this is truly to have ended birth-and-death. The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:

“When an ordinary person is about to die, he has only to contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty, that the four elements are without a self, that the true mind is without marks, neither going nor coming: at birth the nature does not come, at death the nature does not go; clear and perfectly still, mind and objects are one suchness. If one can thus awaken directly and immediately, and is no longer bound by the three times, then one is a person who has transcended the world.”

So if the mind of a sentient being simply lets everything go, it attains great ease. “All that passes before the eyes is sorted into fair and foul; in the end, nothing has anything to do with you.” At any time and in any place: see through (all marks are no-marks) and let go (do not be turned by objects)—see through and let go. The Great Discourse on the Establishing of Mindfulness says: “One has accomplished the state in which there is only knowing and only awareness, has transcended clinging, and no longer covets anything in the world of body and mind.”

This section clarifies why one should be free of marks and dwell nowhere (seeing marks without delusion, not being turned by objects). Because being free of marks and dwelling nowhere brings not only immeasurable merit but also a deeper reason: “All that has marks is illusory and false,” and “if you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata.” In Section Fourteen it is carried further still:
“Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

Yet special care is needed here: being free of marks means not clinging to marks, not annihilating marks. To cling to marks is to fall into existence; to annihilate marks is to fall into emptiness—and this is the common disease of all sentient beings. The correct way is neither to cling to marks nor to annihilate them, but to use illusion to transcend illusion, until illusions are exhausted and the dream ends. Therefore, being without the four marks means being free of these four marks (not clinging to them), not annihilating them; one should use marks without being used by them.
Question: Why is it said that “all that has marks is illusory and false”?
Answer: In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the World-Honored One gives this teaching:
“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another
(misidentifying east, west, south, and north—a metaphor for taking the false as true and the unreal as real)

, wrongly taking the four elements as the mark of their own body and the shadows cast by the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon.”

(“The shadows cast by the six dusts” are the images that arise in dependence on the six dusts—the conceptions and deluded thoughts that arise when the six faculties meet the six dusts. They exist because of the dusts and cease when the dusts cease, and so they are called “shadows.”)

“The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person wrongly clings to them, and because of that wrong clinging he is not only deluded about the nature of this space but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence comes the turning round in birth-and-death, and so it is called ignorance
(because one turns round with objects and vainly undergoes birth-and-death, it is called ignorance)
. This ignorance has no real substance
(ignorance is not truly existent; it is an illusion)
: it is like a person in a dream—while dreaming it is not nothing, but on waking there is nothing to be found at all.”

Many sutras and treatises discuss the dream of ignorance: all sentient beings are within the dream of ignorance, while the buddhas and Tathāgatas, having exhausted the dream of ignorance, freely manifest all kinds of Buddha-work in all worlds of the ten directions to deliver sentient beings. For example:

Great Master Hanshan says: “The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha’s; it is originally undefiled and has no marks of birth, death, coming, or going. But because of initial non-awakening, one is deluded about one’s original self-nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all kinds of deluded thoughts arise, all kinds of inversion, and one creates all kinds of karma, wrongly taking on the suffering of birth-and-death in the three realms. All of this ignorance (all these ignorances), not understanding one’s own mind, follows deluded thoughts and turns: it is like a person in deep sleep having all kinds of nightmares—all kinds of realms, all kinds of terror, sufferings beyond bearing. And when he wakes, he seeks the things of the dream and cannot find them at all. Therefore sentient beings, fallen into the dream of ignorance, turn round with deluded thoughts, create all kinds of karma, and take on all kinds of suffering for themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of those inverted states be found?” (From the Dream Roaming Collection,
“Instructions for Dong Zhiguang”)
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Great, Vast Tathāgata says:
“All Tathāgatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable great and awe-inspiring powers, and even realize entry into the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusions)

, and can manifest all kinds of sovereign deeds in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions. It is like a person who dreams of all kinds of transformed things, and when he awakens, everything he saw is gone. Ordinary people are the same: because of the dream of ignorance they wrongly give rise to the notion that dharmas are real entities. The buddhas, having awakened, cling to nothing, and so in all worlds of the ten directions they can in a single thought manifest immeasurable Buddha-work, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing all sentient beings to accomplishment, causing them all to awaken and enter the immeasurable, profound, and wondrous gates of liberation.”
The Mahāyāna Sutra of Secret Adornment says:
“Like forms in a dream
(the dust of form—things that can be seen)

, they are seen only by deluded thought; on waking they do not exist. In the dream of ignorance one sees all kinds of forms, such as men and women; on attaining perfect enlightenment one sees none of them—just as when the skin and leaves of a banana tree are stripped away, there is no core within.”
The Sutra of the Divination of the Karmic Retribution of Good and Evil says:

“If among such sentient beings there are those who, through the permeation of the Dharma-body, have gained strength, whose afflictions gradually thin, who can grow weary of the world and seek the path of nirvāṇa, who believe and take refuge in the one reality, and who cultivate the six pāramitās and all the dharmas that pertain to enlightenment—such a one is called a bodhisattva. If among such bodhisattvas there are those who, cultivating all good dharmas to fulfillment, ultimately escape the sleep of ignorance, they are then called Buddha.”
It also says:

“Because all virtuous practices are brought to fulfillment, one becomes a Buddha. That is, relying on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, one can remove all obstructions, because the dream of ignorance is exhausted
(because one has awakened from the dream of ignorance)
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra,
Scroll Five Hundred Seventy-Six, says:

“If all sentient beings could truly understand that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, they should long since have realized supreme enlightenment; but because sentient beings cannot comprehend that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, they turn round in birth-and-death within the various destinies. It is as when a magician, by whatever object, conjures up all kinds of conjured things—namely the world, Māra
(short for the god Māra, that is, Māra Pāpīyas, the king of the sixth heaven of the desire realm)
, Brahmā and Śakra
(the Great Brahmā King and Śakra. The Great Brahmā King is the lord of the first dhyāna heaven; Śakra is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven)
, śramaṇas and brahmin ascetics
(referring to renunciants of all other paths)
, nāgas and yakṣas
(that is, yakṣas)
, asuras
(that is, asuras)

, and other assemblies of humans and non-humans—the foolish sort are deluded and cling to them as real, while the wise and the magician know they have no real nature and are merely all kinds of illusory appearances. In this way, although all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, sentient beings are foolish and do not understand: they take what is not existent as existent and what is impermanent as permanent, and make all kinds of discriminations among dharmas, discriminating form or discriminating mind, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the tainted and the untainted—all kinds of discriminations such as these. Because of these discriminations they do not truly know that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, and because they do
not know, they turn round in birth-and-death.”
Great Master Hanshan’s Dream Roaming Collection,
“Reply to Prefect Yuan Cangru,” says:

“In the cultivation of a bodhisattva, even up to the seventh ground, the dream of ignorance has not yet been broken. All the while, teaching and transforming sentient beings and accomplishing pure lands is Buddha-work within a dream. Therefore a bodhisattva of the eighth ground is like one crossing a river in a dream and does not yet abide in awakening; only at Buddhahood is one called greatly awakened. This is stated plainly, fully recorded in the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and clearly evidenced.”
Question: “All that has marks is illusory and false.” Then if I stick a needle into you, does it hurt?

Answer: Of course it hurts, because we are still within the dream of ignorance. If one has awakened from the dream of ignorance, there is no body and no needle either—where then would any hurting or not hurting be? The Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream there are clearly the six destinies; after awakening, all is empty—no trichiliocosm.”

In this section the World-Honored One teaches: those who give rise to right faith in this sutra are most supremely blessed (it is most rare), and they obtain merit and virtue as immeasurable as this! He also points out who is able truly to believe in and uphold the Diamond Sutra.
Subhūti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Will there be many sentient beings who, hearing such words and phrases, give rise to true faith?
Subhūti said to the Buddha”

—Subhūti respectfully asks the Buddha. Wherever this sutra says “Subhūti said to the Buddha,” it is a matter of solemn importance, emphasizing that what is said is most essential. “Said to” is the speech of a subordinate to a superior.
World-Honored One! Will there be many sentient beings who, hearing such words and phrases, give rise to true faith?

”—World-Honored One! Will there be many sentient beings who have the good fortune to hear this truth you have taught—“all that has marks is illusory and false; if you see all marks as no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata”—and will they truly understand it and truly believe it?

[Many sentient beings] A great many sentient beings. [Many] Very, quite; as in “quite of that opinion.” [Words and phrases] The explanations by which the ancients analyzed and studied the classics (such as the Four Books and the Five Classics) were mostly called “chapters and phrases.” Here the two characters “words and phrases” refer to the principles set out above. [True faith] True faith is not vague, drifting belief; one must be able to understand the true meaning of such words and phrases and thereby give rise to faith.

Since beginningless lifetimes, human beings have taken all things to be real; now the World-Honored One declares that all of this is illusion. Subhūti’s wisdom is already opened, so he naturally believes—but will sentient beings be able to believe?

It is like the time before the sixteenth century, when people always believed that the planets and the sun revolved around the earth. When Copernicus, on the basis of astronomical observation, proposed that the planets and the earth all revolve around the sun, people found it hard to accept—and Bruno was even burned to death for holding fast to this truth! When truth comes into conflict with common sense and experience, truth is hard to accept. That is why in Section Fourteen the Buddha says: “If there is again someone who, hearing this sutra, is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such a person is most rare.”
And yet, if one does not know that one is within a deluded dream, how can one ever wake from the deluded dream?

The elder Subhūti of course understood the World-Honored One’s teaching in his heart, but for the sake of sentient beings in the age of the final Dharma, joining compassion and wisdom, he put this question: World-Honored One! Will the sentient beings who have the opportunity to hear such words and phrases give rise to true faith? That is: Will they believe that what you, World-Honored One, have said is true, and also believe that they themselves can uphold and practice it and wake from the deluded dream?

This is the elder, joining compassion and wisdom, clarifying this matter (what kind of person is able to uphold the Diamond Sutra—the principles the World-Honored One has set out above are profoundly deep; must one who can give rise to true faith be of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, or need one not be?). He removes the doubt of us sentient beings whose obstructions are deep and whose wisdom is shallow, so that we do not belittle ourselves and mistakenly suppose our faculties are insufficient, and so miss this opportunity to uphold the sutra that is met but once in a million kalpas. Reading to this point, one feels gratitude beyond words!

The Buddha told Subhūti: Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and they will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, taking them as true.
The Buddha told Subhūti: Do not speak thus!”
The Buddha says to Subhūti: Do not speak in this way! (The World-Honored One’s tone is very weighty.)

After the Tathāgata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and they will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases, taking them as true.”

The teaching above means: after my passage into nirvāṇa, up to the fifth five-hundred-year period and the age of the final Dharma that follows, those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit (they need not be of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, nor broadly learned in the scriptures) will be able to give rise to faith and understand that this is a true saying.
This shows that ordinary people who observe the precepts and cultivate merit in their practice will surely receive the Buddha’s blessing, and so be able to give rise to faith and take this as true.

[After the Tathāgata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years] In the five five-hundred-year periods after the Buddha’s extinction, each period has its own “solidity.” In the first five hundred years, solidity in liberation. At that time the right Dharma flourished; practitioners did not attack other teachings but devoted themselves solely to the Mahāyāna and to benefiting sentient beings, and many attained liberation. In the second five hundred years, solidity in meditative concentration: many practitioners deeply cultivated meditative concentration. In the third five hundred years, solidity in much hearing: practitioners observed the precepts little, were slack in practicing meditative concentration, and prized only much hearing, understanding according to the words. In the fourth five hundred years, solidity in stūpas and temples: practitioners practiced meditative concentration little, delighted in planting fields of merit and broadly forming good connections, and built many stūpas and temples. In the fifth five hundred years, solidity in contention: practitioners did not observe the precepts but prized only contention, increasing wrong views. “After the Tathāgata’s extinction, in the last five hundred years” means the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Tathāgata’s extinction and thereafter. “Cultivating merit” means cutting off evil and accumulating good. Observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for practicing the supramundane Dharma, and so any practitioner who earnestly practices the supramundane Dharma can uphold the Diamond Sutra. [Taking them as true] Believing and honoring this as the truth.

From this we can see that the Diamond Sutra is exceedingly well suited to the practitioners of our time: one need only observe the precepts and cultivate merit, and deeply believe and personally practice, and one can sail with the wind along the bodhi path. We are now in the age of the final Dharma, when sentient beings’ obstructions are deep and their wisdom shallow, yet upholding the Diamond Sutra brings inconceivable merit and virtue, opens wisdom, reveals the true nature of things, and is the most able to break delusion and open awakening. What is more, in “Section Sixteen, Purifying Karmic Obstructions,” the World-Honored One tells us that even those who, because of past offenses, should fall into the evil destinies can uphold the Diamond Sutra and thereby realize the fruit of Buddhahood:

“Good men and good women who uphold, read, and recite this sutra, if they are despised by others, do so because of offenses committed in former lives that should have led them to fall into the evil destinies. Because in this present life they are despised by others, those former offenses are thereby extinguished
, and they shall attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Question: From what has been said above, one need only observe the precepts and cultivate merit to be able to uphold the Diamond Sutra. How then should we understand Section Fifteen, where this sutra is said to be “spoken by the Tathāgata for those who have set out on the Mahāyāna, spoken for those who have set out on the supreme vehicle”?

Answer: Pay special attention to the two occurrences of the word “set out” in this sentence. “Spoken by the Tathāgata for those who have set out on the Mahāyāna, spoken for those who have set out on the supreme vehicle” means: this sutra is spoken by the Tathāgata for those who have formed the intention to uphold the Mahāyāna Dharma, and for those who have formed the intention to uphold the supreme vehicle Dharma. Therefore one looks only at the intention, and does not judge by faculties. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “If one encounters the Tathāgata’s supreme, right path of cultivation toward bodhi, then whether one’s faculties are great or small, all attain the fruit of Buddhahood.” The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records: “The Master (Hung-jen, the Fifth Patriarch of Chan) constantly urged monks and laypeople: simply uphold the Diamond Sutra, and you will see your own nature and straightway realize Buddhahood.”

The World-Honored One’s teaching also tells us: observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for upholding the Diamond Sutra. So when, in upholding the Diamond Sutra, we feel confused and find it hard to begin, this shows that the afflictions of our own mind are coarse and heavy, and we must make up the lesson in observing the precepts and cultivating merit. The Vimalakīrti Sutra,
“The Buddha-Land Chapter,” says: “Observing the precepts is the bodhisattva’s pure land.”

Merit is the practitioner’s provisions on the bodhi path. To walk the path without cultivating merit is to have obstructions and difficulties sprout on every side; when merit and practice support each other, nothing goes against one. Creating evil and receiving calamity comes about through body, speech, and mind; cultivating good and obtaining merit also comes about through body, speech, and mind. Therefore a practitioner should cultivate the ten good karmic paths—this is observing the precepts and cultivating merit, this is the root of studying Buddhism, this is the foundation. The firmer the foundation, the more secure the superstructure; when the foundation is poor, one cannot go on cultivating upward.

Why is it that those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit can “take this as true”? Upāsaka Jiang Weihuang’s Lectures on the Diamond Sutra says: “Some say that observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the root of cultivating prajñā, plugging up the one-sided attachment to emptiness first. That is certainly so, but there is still a doubt. The sutra plainly says ‘taking this as true’—these two kinds of people (the two kinds who observe the precepts and cultivate merit) are, after all, insufficient in knowledge; how could they understand the true essential meaning of this sutra? There is an important principle here. Why is that? Because they receive the Buddha’s blessing. Such people are the faculties chosen and settled by the Buddha: if they can practice in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, observing the precepts and cultivating merit, they will surely receive the Buddha’s blessing, and so be able to take this as true. A student of Buddhism must, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, at every moment, seek the blessing of the Three Jewels. This is so no matter what practice one undertakes. Even when lecturing on the sutras one must set aside one’s ordinary views and seek the blessing of the Three Jewels. To be free of this notion is to have not yet given rise to faith. Take Buddha-recitation: when reciting, one must cast aside all one’s ordinary views and knowledge, so that there is nothing at all in the mind, and single-mindedly seek Amitābha’s blessing; nothing else will do.... When the ancient worthies wrote books, they mostly began with words seeking the blessing of the Three Jewels. When great bodhisattvas composed treatises, they too prefaced them with ‘by the Buddha’s awesome spiritual power.’ This is true and not false; it is not dependence, nor is it superstition. If one lacks such a notion, then a view of self remains, obstructing one’s own spiritual nature—how then could one’s writing of books and treatises be thoroughgoing? Therefore the view of self must be cast aside completely.”

Whether one truly believes the truth taught by the World-Honored One is reflected in our thoughts, speech, and actions; therefore one must closely examine (be aware of) it in body, speech, and mind—this is where the effort lies.

You should know that such a person has planted good roots not merely before one buddha, two buddhas, three, four, or five buddhas, but has already planted all good roots in the presence of immeasurable millions of buddhas.

You should know that these people who “can give rise to faith and take this as true” have planted good roots not merely in the presence of one buddha, two buddhas, three, four, or five buddhas, but have already planted all good roots in the presence of immeasurable millions of buddhas.
[Good roots] The good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because it can produce wondrous fruit, it is called a good root.

In fact, among students of Buddhism, those who have already planted all good roots in the presence of immeasurable millions of buddhas are everywhere. Yet how sad that they fail to accomplish anything in this life, and in the next life there is again the delusion of passing through a womb, so that they cultivate lifetime after lifetime and transmigrate lifetime after lifetime, rising and sinking without end. Whenever one thinks of this, sorrow rises from within, and one feels all the more how precious is the Pure Land Dharma-gate by which anyone can
attain accomplishment in this very life

! Recite the Buddha’s name, and be free of marks (seeing marks without delusion, not being turned by objects); be free of marks, and recite the Buddha’s name—this is the shortcut within shortcuts. (The shortcut within the shortcut!)

That we have now had the good fortune to hear this sutra also shows that we have planted all good roots in the presence of immeasurable millions of buddhas. Were it not so, we could not hear this profoundly deep and wondrous prajñā, and even if we heard it we would not know what we had heard. The good causes of past kalpas cannot be known, but the supreme opportunity of the present must not be lost! If one does not firmly seize this supreme opportunity, but is content to be inferior and gives rise to thoughts of difficulty and obstruction, then even if one has good roots from former lives, they will be cut off by this; once this human body is lost, it is hard to regain for ten thousand kalpas, and one drifts further and further away. Now that we have arrived at the treasure store, on no account return empty-handed—be careful! Be careful! Is there any wise person who, knowing where the treasure lies (knowing that this is the treasure store), would not seek it (would not take the treasure) and go on forever complaining of being orphaned and poor?

The human body is hard to obtain, and present conditions are easily lost. May all who hear this never belittle themselves, but surely join in bringing forth a profound mind, strive and advance, and never let this great opportunity fly past before their eyes and beneath their feet!

Hearing these words and phrases, and even giving rise to a single thought of pure faith—Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that these sentient beings obtain merit and virtue as immeasurable as this.

The World-Honored One says: Hearing these words and phrases, and even giving rise to a single thought of pure faith—Subhūti! I know most clearly and see most clearly that the merit and virtue obtained by these sentient beings is already immeasurable!

[Giving rise to a single thought of pure faith] Wherever one hears it, one suddenly opens and brightens, and thereupon awakens and enters, believing and understanding without doubt, with no obstruction. “A single thought” here means that there is no other thought.
[Pure faith] Truly believing, without the slightest doubt.
The Direct Explanation of the True Mind contains a passage on faith and understanding that is very important for how to practice the Diamond Sutra, excerpted as follows:

The Avataṃsaka says: Faith is the mother of the sources of the Way and of merit; it nurtures and sustains all good roots. And the Consciousness-Only [school] says: Faith is like a pearl of clear water, for it can clarify muddy water. From this we know that faith is the guide that goes before the arising of all good; therefore the Buddhist scriptures place at their head (right at the beginning) “Thus have I heard,” which is precisely for the sake of giving rise to faith.

Someone asks: How does the faith of the ancestral gate (the Chan school) differ from the faith of the teaching gate (the schools of the teachings)? The answer: They differ in many ways. The teaching gate causes gods and humans to believe in cause and effect. Those who love blessings and happiness believe the ten good deeds to be the wondrous cause and rebirth among gods and humans to be the blissful fruit. Those who delight in emptiness and stillness believe arising-and-ceasing causes and conditions to be the right cause and the truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path to be the noble fruit. Those who delight in the fruit of Buddhahood believe the three kalpas (“three kalpas” is short for the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the time a bodhisattva must pass through in cultivating to Buddhahood) and the six pāramitās to be the great cause and bodhi and nirvāṇa to be the right fruit. The right faith of the ancestral gate is not the same as these: it does not believe in any conditioned cause and effect whatsoever, but only believes that one is originally a Buddha, that the innocent, natural self-nature is complete in everyone, and that the wondrous substance of nirvāṇa is perfect in each one, not to be sought from others but present of itself from the very beginning. (This is the basis of the unconditioned Dharma—sentient beings are dreaming the dream of a poor child; one need only wake, and everything is already complete.) The Third Patriarch says: “Perfectly one with great emptiness, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare; it is only because of grasping and rejecting (being deluded by marks and chasing objects) that it is not so.” Master Zhigong says: “Within the body of marks there is the body without marks; on the road of ignorance there is the road without birth.” Yongjia says: “The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.” Therefore we know that sentient beings are originally Buddhas.
